Parent: #2048 (ID Zettelkasten design). Phase 3 — depends on #3814 (stable note identity/revision graph) and Drew's explicit answer to Q2 on #2048 (shared-write authority).

Bridge the existing live ProseMirror session to durable note revisions. Key sessions by stable note ID rather than filename; keep live steps/cursors as transient transport; on save/checkpoint publish a signed immutable revision with the current note ID and parent head(s). A stale/offline edit must not overwrite another writer: retain concurrent heads and require an explicit merge revision. Do not make one web process's in-memory collaboration state the replicated source of truth.

Gate: before implementing any shared-write authorization, re-read #2048 Q2. Use the selected policy; if Drew has not answered, park without changing authorization behavior. Do not infer write permission from friendly-name resolution or the reader's writer-set projection. No cross-store resolver work (that remains #2259).

Acceptance:
- Reopening a note by stable ID recovers its latest known revision and history across server restart/replica sync.
- [x] A normal live session can checkpoint to a signed revision; ephemeral steps/cursors are not emitted as permanent events. Covered by PR #14623; focused Fleet run 45493556312 passed (7 passed, 0 failed).
- [x] Concurrent/offline sessions create separate heads; an explicit merge names its parents; no last-writer-wins data loss in the tested paths. Covered by PR #14623; focused Fleet run 45493556312 and full id-web suite run 45496785776 passed.
- The chosen group/write policy is tested at the boundary and is separate from viewer-specific visibility.
- Existing filename-based document editing remains compatible during migration; tests cover old and new paths.

items.title: story: our own OIDC/SAML/SSO identity provider
items.body:
## User story

As the operator of our own services, I want one self-hosted identity provider issuing OIDC + SAML SSO for our own services — pm-stack, the mcpx and Desktop Commander doors ([#13404 — Desktop Commander front door endpoint](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13404)), OpenChamber, fleet surfaces — so that sign-in across our estate runs on our own identity instead of a patchwork of third-party IdPs and per-service arrangements.

Motivation:

- One identity: the same person, service, and policy across every service, instead of a separate account story per service.
- Our own trust anchor: signing keys and certificates issued from our own PKI, under our own control, instead of trusting a vendor's keys for our own estate.
- No per-service vendor dependency: adding a service means registering a relying party with our provider, not adopting another third-party IdP or inventing a one-off sign-in scheme.

Done at the story level looks like: our provider is the sign-in path for at least one service of each class in the acceptance criteria below, its signing keys come from our PKI and can be rotated without breaking sign-in, and a new service can be onboarded by configuration against our provider rather than by choosing a new identity vendor.

This story does not start from a blank page. It is the story-level frame over the SSO program that already exists — parent issue [#9077 — parent SSO program issue itself](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9077) and its children — plus the PKI foundation and the SAML scope, which the existing program does not cover. The "Prior work and references" section below is the map; the slice plan builds on those pieces rather than re-specifying them.

## Scope + acceptance criteria

- [ ] PKI foundation exists: root CA, an issuing intermediate, and cert-generation tooling (Slice 1).
- [ ] OIDC discovery + JWKS signing works: the provider publishes its discovery document and a JWKS signed from PKI-issued keys.
- [ ] SAML IdP metadata + signing works: the provider publishes signed SAML IdP metadata and signs SAML responses.
- [ ] At least one relying party from each class signs in end-to-end: a web app, and a CLI/API surface.
- [ ] Signing-key rotation is demonstrated: a new signing key is published and trusted, and the old key is retired, without breaking sign-in.
- [ ] Operators can issue and revoke service certificates from the PKI.
- [ ] Provider accounts bind to pkgs/id accounts via the binding ceremony in [#2852 — hosted provisioning SSO ID binding](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2852) (recorded as acceptance debt in the provider child issue, not an afterthought).

## Prior work and references

Search record (2026-11-23, GitHub issue search over developing-today/code, counts confirmed from the search API): `oidc` 222 hits, `saml` 4, `sso` 71, `"identity provider"` 73, `idp` 20, `oauth` 170, `login` 301, `auth` 1185. The `login`/`auth` counts are broad and noisy; the relevant hits are below.

**Plain findings first:**

- **SAML is new ground.** All 4 `saml` hits are the github-backup estate mirror and GitHub-org SAML access — no prior SAML IdP design, issue, or design record found. The SAML scope in this story is genuinely new work, not a re-specification.
- **Number corrections to the original brief for this story:** the Google federated-login issue is [#13412 — Google federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13412), a child of #9077. [#12412 — console gate whole public hostname](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/12412) is a closed PR (the pm-stack console as the gate for the whole public hostname), related to the Access wiring but not itself a Google-login issue. And [#8299 — id roles capability ceiling config](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/8299) is pkgs/id role configuration (capability ceilings, delegation bounds), not mcpx work — the mcpx ceiling/session line is [#1902 — mcpx daemon ceiling caller lowers](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1902), [#1950 — mcpx OAuth authorization conformance work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1950), and the mcpx book's identity chapter (below).

### The existing SSO program — #9077 and its children

- [#9077 — parent SSO program issue itself](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9077) — SSO for fleet services: GitHub/Google/Microsoft login gated to Drew + a devtoday OIDC provider with roles + account linking. This story's OIDC half is that program, framed at story level and extended with PKI + SAML.
- [#13409 — minimal devtoday OIDC provider standup](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13409) — standard OIDC issuer (code + PKCE), JWKS + key rotation, Drew-only allowlist enforced in the provider, #1253 role claims, no id keypair custody in the login path.
- [#13411 — GitHub federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13411)
- [#13412 — Google federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13412)
- [#13414 — Microsoft federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13414)
- [#13415 — account linking flow with history](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13415) — one account, every door, with retained identity history.
- [#13416 — first consumer proving full loop](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13416) — first consumer integration (PM stack) proving the full loop.
- [#13417 — fleet SSO provider decision note](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/13417) — the decision note PR for #9077; it settles the pkgs/id question (see the design questions below). Open at filing time; its design record is `doc/2026-11-23_design_fleet_sso_9077.md` on its branch until merged.
- [#9086 — hosted editions consume SSO design](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9086) — hosted editions are relying parties consuming #9077; tenancy accounts aligned with #1253 roles.
- [#1253 — one identity across the stack](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1253) — SSO propagation from the public entry into every layer; the four-role model (owner / orchestrator / agent / read-only) is the consumer-side contract the provider's claims must carry.
- [#1182 — dashboard behind Cloudflare Access design](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1182) — the settled Access model for the pm-stack entry; the existing door this provider eventually stands behind.
- [#9605 — stack token minting exchange work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9605) — stack-token minting + agent token-exchange under #1253; how an entry session becomes per-layer tokens.

### pkgs/id — the existing identity system

- [#2056 — ID platform expansion epic home](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2056) — the ID program epic; pkgs/id is Drew's identity system (Iroh-key identity, id-caps capabilities, directory, groups).
- [#2852 — hosted provisioning SSO ID binding](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2852) — external SSO identities bound to pkgs/id accounts (spec source #2258); slices 1–2 landed, 3–4 open at last record in #9077.
- [#5684 — identity login delegation design work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5684) — identity, login & delegation: key custody, security-code recovery, pseudo-login identities. Its custody questions are unresolved, which is part of why the provider does not start inside id.
- [#2060 — key recovery versus SSO loss](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2060) — the standing rule from the key-recovery investigation: SSO authenticates a person to an account record; it never rebinds an identity key.
- [#2380 — keyset authorization log identity substrate](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2380) — device keys, revocation, and bindings as signed records; the revocation/rotation substrate Slice 5 builds on.
- [#8299 — id roles capability ceiling config](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/8299) — roles as first-class world config: capability ceiling, delegation-lifetime bounds, grant/revoke as audited events. The id-side role/ceiling model the provider's roles must not silently diverge from.

### Doors, mcpx, and fleet token auth — worked examples and neighbours

- [#13404 — Desktop Commander front door endpoint](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13404) — Worker front door, Access gate, laptop bridge.
- [#13488 — OAuth front door shipped implementation](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/13488) — merged PR: OAuth 2.1 front door for hosted MCP clients (`pkgs/desktop-commander/worker/src/oauth.ts`). The in-house worked example of the OAuth pattern.
- [#12417 — Google OAuth client creation task](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/12417) — the Google OAuth client for pm.security.cab; the concrete Google-side wiring the Access door runs on today (closed).
- [#12412 — console gate whole public hostname](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/12412) — closed PR: the pm-stack console is the gate for the whole public hostname.
- [#1950 — mcpx OAuth authorization conformance work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1950) — mcpx as OAuth client / resource server. Per `doc/fleet/mcpx-oauth-authorization-server.md` (decision 2026-10-28), mcpx does **not** embed an authorization server — it points at external ones. This provider is the external server it points at.
- [#13657 — mcpx public endpoint front door](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13657) — mcpx public endpoint with an OAuth/Google-SSO front door and machine bearer; a first-class relying party candidate for this provider.
- [#1902 — mcpx daemon ceiling caller lowers](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1902) — the capability-ceiling mechanism (daemon sets, caller may lower, never raise) that provider-issued policy/session claims must respect.
- [#5343 — laptop agent resident execution design](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5343) and [#5362 — queue secrets brokers laptop design](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5362) — the fleet/laptop-agent token-auth line: brokered, token-gated laptop services reached only through the session proxy. The machine-to-machine auth pattern the provider's CLI/API relying parties should align with, not replace casually.
- [#9158 — fleet CA canonical secrets model](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9158) — fleet-ca canonical secrets model, provider adapters & custody policy; adjacent to Slice 1's PKI — the CA program links #9077 and does not absorb it (per its design record below), and this story returns the favour.

### Design records (repo `doc/`)

- `doc/2026-11-23_design_fleet_sso_9077.md` — the #9077 decision note (via PR #13417, on branch until merged): settles separate-minimal-provider-first, with an explicit fold path into pkgs/id.
- `doc/2026-10-30T22-45-00Z_design_hosted_provisioning_sso_binding.md` — hosted provisioning + SSO→ID binding spec (#2258 line): Google SSO authenticates the account; the Iroh root key is the identity.
- `doc/2026-10-28T23-34-14Z_investigation_cloudflare_workers_fit/` — §4: Google SSO on Workers and binding a Google identity to an ID identity; "SSO is the door; the ID key remains the identity"; custodial keys rejected.
- `doc/2026-10-29T11-28-18Z_investigation_key_recovery_hosted/` — key recovery for hosted users; verified at the time that pkgs/id contained no Google/OIDC/OAuth/WebAuthn code — all SSO content was specification.
- `doc/2026-11-10T23-58-00Z_design_pm_stack_identity/` — the #1253 design record: Access JWT at the entry, short-lived stack tokens per layer, roles in the aggregator registry, "the central OIDC provider (#9077)".
- `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2046.md` + `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2283.md` — hosted-edition identity designs; they record an unresolved conflict with the Oct 30 SSO spec (`binding_id` vs `sub` as the store key) that the design pass must reconcile, not rediscover.
- `doc/fleet/mcpx-oauth-authorization-server.md` — mcpx embed-vs-point-at decision: hybrid, point-at-first; mcpx never issues tokens, it validates other issuers' tokens via JWKS.
- `doc/2026-11-13T01-34-11Z_design_fleet_ca_credentials_secrets/` — the fleet CA / credentials / secrets program: its note links #9077 as an adjacent relying-party/identity program it does not absorb; its spec (§27) already compares Keycloak / Authentik / Kanidm / Zitadel for a standalone SSO platform — the build-vs-adopt design pass starts from that comparison, not from zero.
- `doc/2026-11-12T19-10-07Z_design_keyset_authorization_log/` — the #2380 keyset/authorization-log design.
- `pm-stack/console/README.md` — records today's wiring plainly: `google.access-sso` OAuth client secrets, the Access sign-in method, and "the central OIDC provider (#9077)" as the intended provider.

### The four books

- **id book** (`pkgs/id/book/`): `concepts/identity-directory.md` (Identity, the directory and groups), `concepts/capabilities.md` (Capabilities, ceilings and providers), `design/identity-directory-groups.md` (identity, directory, groups and delegation), `design/hosted-editions.md` (hosted and serverless editions), `design/capabilities-providers.md`. This is where id's identity model is written down as a book, and the fold-path design must be written against it.
- **mcpx book** (`pkgs/mcpx/docs/`): `spec/identity.md` ("Who an MCP request is from"), `compare/register/auth.md` (the authorization register: OIDC discovery, PKCE, issuer checks), `decisions/0007-elicitation-identity.md` (elicitation binds no user identity), and the auth rows of `spec/conformance-matrix.md`.
- **fleet book** (`pkgs/fleet/book/`): `concepts/proxy.md` (Proxy, sessions and recovery) and `reference/queue-dispatch.md` are the closest chapters — the fleet book covers sessions and tokens as transport, and **no dedicated SSO/identity chapter was found in the fleet book**.
- **atlas book** (`pkgs/atlas-search/book/`): `design/fleet-and-id-integration.md` and `design/access-evolution.md` touch ID integration and access evolution; **no prior dedicated identity, federation, or sign-in design was found in the atlas book**.

### Sandbox-side notes

- `~/memory/topics/id-program-2026-10-28.md` — Drew's ID program directive: the Workers edition signs in via Google SSO, Google `sub` is the SSO key, custodial keys rejected.
- Standing operator practice (memory, 2026-10-24): SSO-first sign-ins for Drew's own service accounts — operator practice, not IdP design, listed here so the two are not conflated.
- No SAML material was found in the sandbox notes either — consistent with the GitHub search: SAML is new ground on every front searched.

## Open design questions — options and chosen defaults

Chosen defaults below are recorded under Drew's decision posture: prefer options, "both" where both can coexist, and the more capable option over the most locked-down or most basic. Where a prior decision already exists, it is recorded as the chosen default rather than re-decided.

### 0. Relationship to pkgs/id — the central question

pkgs/id **is** an identity system (Iroh-key identity, capabilities, directory, groups; epic #2056). Any new provider has to state its relationship to it:

- **Option A — Same system:** pkgs/id itself becomes the OIDC/SAML provider.
- **Option B — A layer over it:** a thin OIDC/SAML protocol layer whose accounts and keys are id accounts and id keys throughout.
- **Option C — Deliberately separate first, with a fold path:** a separate minimal provider now; provider accounts later bind to id accounts via the #2852 ceremony, with an explicit path for the provider to fold into id.
- **CHOSEN: Option C — separate minimal provider first, explicit fold path into pkgs/id.** This is the decision already recorded in the #9077 decision note (PR #13417; Drew may override per §5 of that note). Reasoning, from #9077's own evidence: no OIDC surface exists in pkgs/id, #5684's key-custody model is unresolved and more exotic than a conventional issuer, #2852's binding slices 3–4 are open — while fleet services need boring, standard OIDC first. Two standing constraints bind whichever option the design pass lands on: no id keypair custody in the login path (#13409), and SSO never rebinds an id key (#2060).

### 1. Build vs adopt

- **Option A — Hand-build:** build the IdP ourselves on our own components.
- **Option B — Adopt-and-package:** adopt an existing IdP core (e.g. Keycloak-class), package and run it ourselves, fronted by our own PKI.
- **CHOSEN: Option B — adopt-and-package.** Identity protocols are high-risk to hand-roll; our differentiation is the PKI and the integrations, not the protocol code. Note for the design pass: this must be reconciled with Question 0's "separate **minimal** provider" — the fleet CA program's spec already compares Keycloak / Authentik / Kanidm / Zitadel (see Prior work), and the pass must show the adopted core can stay minimal (Drew-only gate, #1253 role claims, PKI-issued signing keys) rather than assuming it.

### 2. Where it runs

- **Option A — Laptop-hosted only:** run the provider as a service on the laptop.
- **Option B — A fleet surface only:** run the provider on a fleet surface.
- **Option C — Both, laptop primary:** run it laptop-hosted first, with a fleet surface as the same provider's second home / reach path, laptop primary.
- **CHOSEN: Option C — both, laptop primary.** It starts where our execution already lives, without closing off a fleet home when reach needs it. (Open sub-question for the design pass: the hosted/Workers edition line under #9077's relatives is a third home candidate — the pass should address it explicitly rather than this story guessing.)

### 3. How relying parties integrate

- **Option A — Direct per service:** each service is configured directly for OIDC/SAML against the provider.
- **Option B — Via the door Workers:** the existing door Workers act as relying-party proxies in front of services.
- **CHOSEN: Both A and B.** They can coexist — direct config where a service supports it well, door Workers as proxies where a service needs a door in front of it. PR #13488's Commander door is the worked example of B; #9086 is the design home for hosted editions consuming the provider directly (A).

### 4. Signing-key rotation

- **Option A — Manual ceremony:** rotation is a deliberate, manual operator ceremony.
- **Option B — Automated rollover:** automated rollover with overlapping JWKS publication, so old and new keys are both trusted during the changeover.
- **CHOSEN: Option B — automated rollover with overlapping JWKS publication.** Overlap makes rotation routine instead of an outage risk, which is what makes rotating often practical. This is already in #13409's scope ("JWKS + key rotation"); Slice 5 proves it rather than designing it from scratch.

### 5. Relationship to the existing Access / Google SSO wiring

Related, not duplicated here: [#13412 — Google federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13412) and [#13411 — GitHub federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13411) / [#13414 — Microsoft federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13414) (the federated logins under #9077), [#12417 — Google OAuth client creation task](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/12417) (today's Google client for pm.security.cab), and [#13404 — Desktop Commander front door endpoint](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13404) (the Commander OAuth door).

- **Option A — Rip-and-replace:** remove the existing Access/Google wiring and replace it with this provider in one move.
- **Option B — Stand behind the doors:** keep the existing doors and wiring in place, and make this provider the identity standing behind those doors, taking over from Google as the upstream identity over time.
- **CHOSEN: Option B — stand behind the doors, not a rip-and-replace.** The doors our services already use keep working; what changes is whose identity is behind them. This matches #9077's own shape: GitHub/Google/Microsoft stay as federated logins **into** our provider, gated and linked to one account — Google goes from being the identity to being one door into ours.

## Slice plan — in dependency order

1. **Slice 1 — PKI foundation:** cert-generation tooling + root CA + issuing intermediate. *Executed in parallel by the PKI foundation work, 2026-11-23, alongside the filing of this story.* Builds alongside the fleet-ca program ([#9158 — fleet CA canonical secrets model](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9158) and its design record above) rather than re-specifying a CA model.
2. **Slice 2 — Signing keys:** signing keys for OIDC (JWKS) and SAML, issued from the PKI — the keys [#13409 — minimal devtoday OIDC provider standup](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13409) already scopes as "JWKS + key rotation", now sourced from our PKI instead of provider-local generation.
3. **Slice 3 — The provider itself:** the provider stood up per #13409 + the #9077 children (#13411 / #13412 / #13414 federated logins, #13415 account linking), publishing OIDC discovery/JWKS — **plus SAML IdP metadata + signing, which is new work with no prior design (see Prior work) and needs its own design slice in the design pass.**
4. **Slice 4 — Per-service integrations:** [#13416 — first consumer proving full loop](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13416) (PM stack) first, the Commander door pattern (PR #13488) for Worker-fronted services, and mcpx as a pointing-at relying party per its authorization-server decision ([#1950 — mcpx OAuth authorization conformance work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1950), [#13657 — mcpx public endpoint front door](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13657)) — one per service class first, then the remaining services.
5. **Slice 5 — Rotation + revocation drills:** demonstrate signing-key rotation (overlapping JWKS, per Question 4) and certificate revocation end-to-end, building on the keyset/authorization-log substrate ([#2380 — keyset authorization log identity substrate](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2380)) instead of inventing a parallel revocation story.

## Closing note

This issue is the design-mill intake (starter issue) for the identity program, so it can route into a full design pass next. The design pass's first job is reconciliation, not invention: the #9077 decision note, the `binding_id` vs `sub` conflict recorded in the id hosted-edition designs, the build-vs-adopt vs minimal-provider tension in Questions 0–1, and the SAML scope, which has no prior art in the repo.

items.title: Repo sweep 2026-11-23: leftovers holding unlanded or unjudged state
items.body:
Filed by the 2026-11-23 repo sweep (all repos/worktrees in sandbox + laptop homes). The sweep landed what it safely could and deleted 213 verified-done worktrees. The items below were deliberately left in place because they hold state that exists nowhere else or needs an owner's judgment. Nothing here was discarded.

## 1. Queue-task worktrees with local-only tip commits (largest class)
~200 worktrees under `~/git/fleet/` and sibling areas (code parent: 133 in the fleet bucket alone; opencode parent: 44; openchamber parent: 24) are clean but their HEAD commit is on NO remote ref — typically 1–2 commits from Nov 7–11 task runs. Sampling shows the class is MIXED: `fleet/11051-6831`'s tip is patch-equivalent to landed work (`git cherry` `-`), but `fleet/11065-6847`'s two commits (fix + property tests for #6847) are NOT in main in that form (`git cherry` `+`). Do not bulk-delete; each needs a cherry check or an owner decision.

## 2. Code primary's preserved local commits
`~/git/code` primary had 2 unpushed local commits on main (incl. Drew-authored `73e6f743` "model", 2026-11-23 17:57: `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` route config + `pm-stack/opencode-claimant` changes). Preserved verbatim on pushed branch `archer/repo-sweep-primary-snapshot`; primary reset to origin/main, clean. Judgment needed:
- claimant.py contains ONE novel hunk not in main (classify a well-formed `{"task": null}` answer with exit 5 as `no_match`, not `cli_nonzero`, in `_collect_handed_offs`) mixed with hunks that are OLDER than main (would regress `hand_back_step`/`launch_step`). Port the novel hunk; do not merge the commit as-is.
- The opencode.jsonc portion is route/model config from Drew's own session — owner's call.

## 3. opencode primary is mid-merge

items.body:
## Evidence

PR #14497 (for #14391) refuses filter and order columns that are reserved PostgREST parameter names or not plain identifiers. The projection path is still unchecked:

- `pkgs/id/crates/id-pg/src/translate.rs` `resolve_projection` (around step 8) expands the query's `select` against `declared_columns` and joins the names into the `select` parameter (step 10: `projection.join(",")`).
- `CollectionAllowlist` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-pg/src/allowlist.rs`) accepts any string as a declared column name, so a declared column such as `a,b`, `x(y)`, or `or` lands raw in the `select` value.
- `path: format!("/{relation}")` is also raw; #14497 refuses a non-identifier relation at translate time, but nothing refuses it at allowlist construction.

## Why it matters

The translator is the only guard until the transport (#13763) makes live calls. A declared name with `,`, `(`, `)`, `"` or whitespace changes the shape of the `select` list the source parses. Refusing at construction time means a bad config never reaches a request.

## Suggested fix

1. Add `CollectionAllowlist::validate(&self) -> Result<(), String>` in `allowlist.rs`: relation is a plain identifier; every declared column name is a plain identifier and not reserved (`is_usable_field_name`); `unique_key` entries are declared columns.
2. Call it from registration (#13758) when the allowlist is built, and from `Translator::new` in debug builds or as a `Result`-returning constructor.
3. In `resolve_projection`, refuse with `field_unsupported` if a declared column fails `is_usable_field_name`, as defense in depth.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `cargo test -p id-pg` in `pkgs/id` passes.
- [ ] Unit test: a collection declaring column `a,b` fails `validate()`; a declared `or` fails `validate()`; a declared plain column passes.
- [ ] Unit test: a `select *` query against a collection with a declared column `x(y)` is refused as `field_unsupported` (no `select` parameter emitted).
- [ ] Refusal bodies stay byte-identical for withheld and unknown columns (existing `withheld_and_unknown_columns_produce_identical_bodies` still passes).
- [ ] Doc comment on `validate` states which names are rejected and why.

## Dependencies

- Builds on PR #14497 (for #14391): `is_usable_field_name` and `is_plain_identifier`. Blocked-by that PR merging.
- Feeds registration #13758.

items.body:
## Summary

Research + design for **forking a Rust KDL stack for ID**, extending #5688
(KDL → JSON → atomic triples → SQL/PGQ). This issue runs Drew's KDL
thread to ground in three directions:

1. **Archaeology (laptop hunt):** the missing KDL material Drew
   remembered exists — it is `pkgs/mappy/migrations/limit.kdl`, his
   Dec-2023 scratchpad, and it is the concrete ancestor of #5688's
   triples design.
2. **Archaeology (upstream):** Drew's actual capability asks to the KDL
   project were found — two GitHub Discussions in `kdl-org/kdl`
   (**#344 Children Annotation**, **#362 Property Annotation**, both
   Dec-2023) that were **not adopted** into KDL 2.0. Together with his
   spec-era comments and his Go-ecosystem work (kdl-go, koanf), they
   define the fork's extension list.
3. **Fork base:** fork **`kdl-org/kdl-rs`** (the `kdl` crate, v6.7.1) —
   the only maintained, format-preserving, dual-version (1.0 + 2.0)
   Rust KDL document parser, with serde and KQL built in. The
   annotation generalization Drew wants is a contained AST change
   there, and a rebuild-everything proposition anywhere else.

Umbrella: epic #2056. Parent design: #5688 (this issue supplies its
parser/implementation substrate and its annotation model).

---

## 1. Laptop hunt — what was searched, what was found

Searched (2026-11-04, laptop online): every `*.kdl` file under the
laptop home (deduped across the many worktrees/clones), plus content
greps for "kdl" over the laptop's zettel corpus (`~/git/zettel`),
cairn (`~/git/cairn`), hatch-personal, and notes trees
(`~/hatch/notes`, `~/git/fleet/notes`, `~/queue-notes`).

**Not covered / honest gaps:** the dozens of repo worktrees are clones
of the same trees (deduplicated, not re-read); the Atlas local chunk
store was not mined for documents; no ChatGPT `conversations.json`
export exists on the laptop (the late-2023 prose brainstorming remains
unrecovered — the #5688 follow-on stands).

### 1.1 The find: `pkgs/mappy/migrations/limit.kdl` (106 lines, Drew, 2023-12-17)

A design scratchpad inside the `mappy` graph/triples experiment
(Python + SQL migrations; cf. `node.sql`, `crdb.sql` beside it).
Committed 2023-12-17 — **the same day** as upstream discussion #362
below. Its key positions, verbatim in spirit:

- **Triples modeled as annotations** — the direct ancestor of #5688 §2:

  ```kdl
  (subject)character "Brian" {
      (predicate)"writesBooks" (object)"Wish It, Want It, Do It" (object)"Faster Than the Speed of Love"
      (predicate)"travelsWith" (object)"Stewie" (object)"Peter"
  }
  ```

- **Parameterized / structured annotation payloads** — far beyond the
  spec's single bare identifier:

  ```kdl
  (predicate#NotVeryWell)"writesBooks" (object#book#author:BrianGriffin)"Wish It, Want It, Do It"
  (object::Baby:Lois'sBaby::Kind-Of-Annoying)"Stewie" (object:FamilyGuy)"Peter"
  (yes:yes:no:::bool)"=" "yes" "no" "yes"
  (document:object)rdf { ... }
  ```

- **Annotations on every part** — node names, argument values (and, in
  the commented-out variant, `(subject)character="Brian"` prop-style
  modeling), plus experiments that leave the grammar entirely
  (`` `=(predicate) ``, `:=(object)"examples"`, annotations embedded in
  comments `/*(result)*/`).
- **The triples store sketched in comments**, Dec-2023:

  ```
  // nodes: id, type, key, value
  // links: id, type, from, to
  // meta_links: id, type, from, to
  ```

- An RDF / Dublin-Core record re-expressed in KDL under
  `(document:object)rdf`, and a tail of deliberate lexical torture
  tests (quote/escape/emoji edge cases) — parser-robustness probing.

This file is why the fork's annotation design (§4b) treats the
annotation slot as *structured data*, not a bare tag.

### 1.2 Other real KDL material on the laptop (all in `developing-today/code`)

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `pkgs/roc/out-in.kdl` (39 ln) | Roc syntax brainstorm in KDL form (known fragment; links kdl-play) |
| `pkgs/roc/platform.kdl` (14 ln) | Prose platform notes as KDL strings |
| `pkgs/identity/config.kdl` + `pkgs/identity/configuration/embed/config.kdl` | Production identity-service config written in KDL |
| `~/.config/zellij/config.kdl` | Tool config (zellij) — not Drew's design material |

### 1.3 Negative results

- No KDL documents or design notes in the laptop zettel / cairn /
  notes corpora (one `flake.lock` substring hit only).
- `developing-today/hygge` (GitHub, 2022) is Drew's builder-only Rust
  KDL crate ("knuffel or kdl-rs for deserialization :-)"); its
  `SPEC.md` is a vendored copy of the KDL 1.0 grammar. It is prior art
  for the *serializer* half of our stack, not a parser base.

---

## 2. Drew's KDL-ecosystem threads — the capability-ask catalogue

Method: GitHub search (`author:` / `commenter:` / `involves:`) across
the `kdl-org` org and globally for "kdl", plus a full pass over
`kdl-org/kdl` **Discussions** via GraphQL (search does not index
Discussions — that is where the headline asks were hiding). All
threads below verified by reading them.

### 2.1 The two declined capability asks (define the fork)

| Thread | Date | Ask | Maintainer response | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [kdl-org/kdl discussion #344 — Children Annotation](https://github.com/kdl-org/kdl/discussions/344) | 2023-11-29 | "Allow annotating the children block in the same way that values and identifiers can be annotated." | tabatkins (spec editor): unconvinced — a node has only one child list, so the information "can just be expressed with a property or attribute"; asked for a use case. | **Not adopted.** KDL 2.0 grammar has no children annotation. |
| [kdl-org/kdl discussion #362 — Property Annotation](https://github.com/kdl-org/kdl/discussions/362) | 2023-12-17 | "Allow annotating properties in the same way that values and identifiers can be annotated." Drew supplied precedents: Go's `lunjon/gokdl` already implements `Prop.TypeAnnot` (`(author)name="Jonathan"`); Elixir's Kuddle supports it too (with `annotations: []` — a *list*). | tabatkins: parseable, but questions the value — keys are unique per node, so "all necessary context is already baked into their name"; asked for a use case. | **Not adopted.** KDL 2.0 grammar: `prop := string '=' value` — no key annotation. |

The irony the design should record: the use cases the maintainers
asked for existed the same week in `limit.kdl` (§1.1) — repeated names
disambiguated by role (`(subject)` / `(predicate)` / `(object)`,
parameterized `(object#book#author:BrianGriffin)`) — exactly the
"same name, different role" rationale the spec itself accepts for
node annotations, extended to every part.

### 2.2 Spec-era participation (KDL 2.0 design batch, Nov-2023)

| Thread | Drew's position | Outcome in KDL 2.0 |
|---|---|---|
| [kdl-org/kdl #343 — prefix keywords with `#`](https://github.com/kdl-org/kdl/issues/343) | Came around to supporting; asked whether `#` would be banned from identifiers / first-char, noting quoted names as the escape. | **Adopted:** 2.0 keywords are `#true` / `#false` / `#null`. |
| [kdl-org/kdl #342 — multiline comments in more places](https://github.com/kdl-org/kdl/issues/342) | "i think this should be legal, i don't know what it should do." | Partially adopted: 2.0 relaxed comment placement (e.g. `//` immediately followed by newline; comments in more positions). |
| [kdl-org/kdljs #21 — KDL 2.0 compliance](https://github.com/kdl-org/kdljs/issues/21) | 2024-12-29: nudged for a 2.0 update post-release (playground dependency). | Closed. |

### 2.3 Implementation-era threads (Go ecosystem, Dec-2023 → Apr-2024)

Drew was simultaneously *building on* KDL — a KDL config provider for
koanf, via kdl-go — and pressing the permissiveness philosophy the
fork inherits:

| Thread | Ask / work | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| [sblinch/kdl-go #3](https://github.com/sblinch/kdl-go/issues/3) (authored) | Marshal panic on lists in `map[string]any`; discovered the `key=val` prop-coercion; asked "is there a toggle somewhere?" and for an error instead of a panic. | Fixed upstream (kdl-go list-marshal fix; Drew pulled it via koanf #267). |
| [sblinch/kdl-go #4](https://github.com/sblinch/kdl-go/issues/4) (authored) | Data-model fidelity cluster: empty nodes unmarshal as `nil` vs empty map; duplicate node names with changing types should be last-wins, not an error; `{ "" 5 ; "" 6 ; }` children mishandled; quoted `"1"` / empty-string identifiers vs bare-identifier rules; **asked for behavior flags/toggles "to extend what is permissible past spec."** | Maintainer asked for isolated test cases; thread closed with "Fixed in 3d5e45f" (2024-04-09). Partially addressed. |
| [knadh/koanf #265 / #266](https://github.com/knadh/koanf/issues/266) (authored) + [developing-today-forks/koanf PR #1, PR #3](https://github.com/developing-today-forks/koanf/pull/1) | Contributed a KDL parser provider for koanf (Go config library); negotiated the `emptyIsNil` difference generically rather than special-casing KDL in tests. | PRs merged in his fork; koanf gained its KDL parser from this work. |
| [knadh/koanf #267](https://github.com/knadh/koanf/issues/267) (authored) | kdl-go dependency update carrying the #3 fix. | Closed. |
| typestreamio/typestream #77 | Commented (local-data joins for stream filtering; libsql-as-file/URL). Tangential to KDL design. | Open; listed for completeness. |

Coverage caveat: issue/PR search + both ends of the Discussions list
were covered; comments Drew may have left inside *other people's*
discussions were not exhaustively enumerated.

### 2.4 The spec baseline (verified against both grammars)

Type annotations in **KDL 1.0** (SPEC_v1: "a prefix to any Node Name
or Value"; `prop := identifier '=' value`; `type := '(' identifier ')'`)
and **KDL 2.0** (IETF-draft grammar: `value := type? …`,
`prop := string '=' value`, `type := '(' string ')'`):

- node names: **one** optional annotation ✔
- argument values & property values: **one** optional annotation ✔
- property keys: **none** ✘ (Drew's #362)
- children blocks: **none** ✘ (Drew's #344)
- multiple annotations anywhere: **none** — the grammar's `type?` is
  singular, everywhere. (Kuddle's `annotations: []` shows at least one
  implementation already models it as a list.)

---

## 3. Rust KDL landscape — fork candidates

Verified 2026-11-04 against crates.io + the repos' current sources.

| | `kdl` (kdl-org/kdl-rs) | `knuffel` (tailhook) | `kaydle` (Lucretiel) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Version / state | **6.7.1**, actively maintained (repo pushed 2026-10; ~2.96M downloads) | 3.2.0, last release **2023-04** (stale) | 0.2.0, last release **2022-07** (unmaintained) |
| Role | Document parser + API; formatting/whitespace/comment-**preserving** parse & modify | Derive-based config decoder (serde-like `Decode`) | Serde ser/de layer *on top of* the `kdl` crate |
| Spec versions | **2.0 default; 1.0 via `v1` feature** (sibling `kdlv1` crate); converts documents between versions | 1.0 only | Whatever the underlying `kdl` crate did in 2022 (1.0 era) |
| Serde | **Built in** (`serde` default feature; `de.rs`/`se.rs`) | Is itself a derive stack (not serde) | Is itself serde — superseded by kdl-rs's built-in serde |
| Search/query | **KQL built in** (`query.rs` — the KDL Query Language) | None | None |
| Annotation model | `KdlNode.ty: Option<KdlIdentifier>`; `KdlEntry.ty: Option<KdlIdentifier>` (value); prop key = bare `KdlIdentifier` (**no slot**); `KdlIdentifier` = value+repr only | Annotations not first-class (consumed as Rust types during decode); no document fidelity | Inherits kdl's AST of its era |
| Round-trip of unknown annotations | Preserved **where representable** (node/value `ty` + full format preservation); structurally impossible for prop keys / multiples — the parser cannot even hold them | N/A (decode discards) | N/A |
| License | Apache-2.0 | MIT/Apache-2.0 | MPL-2.0 |

Also noted: `kdlv1` (the split-out 1.0 implementation kdl 6.x wraps)
and Drew's own `hygge` (builder-only serializer; a candidate to revive
for the output side, §4d).

### Recommendation: fork `kdl-org/kdl-rs` (`kdl` crate)

- It is the **only** candidate that is simultaneously: maintained,
  dual-version, format-preserving, serde-complete, and query-equipped
  (KQL matters for #5688's "searches efficiently" goal).
- The fork's core change is **contained**: generalize
  `ty: Option<KdlIdentifier>` → annotation lists, and add annotation
  slots where the AST has none (prop keys, children blocks). Every
  other subsystem (dual parsers, fmt preservation, serde, KQL,
  miette spans) carries over.
- Starting from knuffel means rebuilding 2.0 support, document
  fidelity, and a serializer from zero; kaydle is a layer, not a
  parser, and is abandoned. Neither survives contact with §4a.
- Apache-2.0; track upstream (spec evolution, test suites — including
  the official KDL test suite the crate already runs) and upstream
  what is upstreamable.

---

## 4. Fork design commitments (Drew, 2026-11-04)

**(a) Compatibility is absolute.** Every valid KDL 1.0 document parses
with its spec meaning unchanged; KDL 2.0 likewise, and future spec
versions are tracked. Extensions are **additive**: they never change
the meaning of a spec-valid document. (A document using extensions is
a superset document — a strict parser may reject it, and that is
accepted; the spec-valid subset always round-trips as plain KDL.)

**(b) Universal, multiple, structured annotations.** Generalize the
spec's value-only type hint to **every part**: node name, each
argument, property **keys**, property values, and the **children
block** (the #344/#362 asks), with **multiple annotations per part**
(Kuddle's `annotations: []` precedent). Open design question, with
`limit.kdl` as the evidence base: annotation **payloads** — Drew's
practice packs structure into the annotation (`#`-/`:`-separated
parameters: `(object#book#author:BrianGriffin)`,
`(yes:yes:no:::bool)`). Decide whether the payload stays an opaque
string (spec-shaped, maximally compatible) or gains a structured
sub-grammar in our dialect, and how either form decomposes into
triples under #5688.

**(c) Performance and search efficiency are first-class.** The
triples pipeline (#5688 §2) parses at ingest scale: streaming /
zero-copy parse paths where they matter, no format-preservation tax
on the hot path (make preservation opt-in per parse), and the
query story (KQL today; the SQL/PGQ graph layer in #5688) designed
against parsed-structure indexes rather than re-parse-per-query.

**(d) Output beyond KDL text — the document-language direction.**
Long-term this stops claiming to be KDL: it is *our document
language* with KDL as its default text form. Required renderers, in
#5688 §1.2's conversion-contract terms: KDL text (default), **JSON**,
**YAML**, and an **LLM sentence rendering** (a document rendered as
prose a model — or a person skimming — can read). Files are produced
"with an option": the same underlying document emits the requested
form. `hygge` (§1.3) is the in-house precedent for the builder/output
half.

## 5. Follow-on questions for the design pass

1. Annotation payload grammar (§4b) — opaque vs structured; triple
   decomposition of parameterized annotations.
2. Extension marking: does a document declare itself extended (a
   header annotation? a version node?), so tooling can warn before a
   strict-KDL consumer chokes?
3. Serde shape for annotation lists (attribute-style in derives?) and
   how the kdl-rs serde layer exposes prop-key annotations.
4. Which pieces, if any, get proposed back upstream (the Discussions
   show the maintainers' objection was use-case-shaped, and we now
   have the use cases — but the fork does not block on upstream).
5. Benchmarks: upstream `kdl` vs fork on the ingest corpus; the
   acceptance bar for §4c.

— Filed by the KDL research pass, 2026-11-04. Sources: laptop
(`~/git/code` primary checkout), GitHub (issues/PRs/Discussions via
search + GraphQL), crates.io, spec grammars (SPEC_v1 + the KDL 2.0
IETF draft) — all read directly during the pass.

## Relationship to the queue programme

Sibling programme to #14158 (queue reprioritization programme 2026-11-24). This programme's outcomes feed #14158's pass-3 band audit: every task created here enters the queue under the same priority law, and blocker-chain escalations here are inputs to its reorder.

Every open PR in every repo Drew owns/admins. Opening snapshot (search API, 2026-11-24 ~07:10Z): dezren39 388, developing-today 174 (of which this repo 118), developing-today-forks 32, plus the long-tail orgs — full census lands as the first record on this issue. PRs in repos Drew does NOT own are listed separately and not merged.

## Per-PR outcomes (exactly one each)

1. **Merge** — verified ready: diff reviewed, no unresolved conflict, does what its issue says. CI runs on main only; verification is diff + linked-issue acceptance + warranted checks. Never force-push main.
2. **Fix and merge** — small mechanical gap (conflict rebase, stale branch, trivial failing piece) fixed in a worktree via the standard routes, then merged.
3. **Priority queue task** — real work remains: a packet naming the PR, its issue(s), what blocks it, and the fix scope, at a priority set by the rules below.

immediate 5 / now 10 / critical 20 / urgent 30 / very high 40 / high 50 / medium 60 / low 70 / very low 80 / minimal 90.

- An item that isn't being worked gets its priority increased (number lowered).
- A blocked item: its blocker chain is prioritized in order — everything needed to unlock is escalated, with the PR's own item next behind its last blocker.
- Questions are reviewed aggressively: a question answerable from Drew's recorded decisions or standing statements is answered, not left waiting. A truly immovable blocker is SPLIT OUT into its own issue/task (its question priority raised); everything that can move is handled and prioritized now.

- PRs #13234 and #13237 are recorded hard skips — held, never merged or modified.

- A PR with a live claim by a working lane is reviewed and routed (task/priority/notes), never stomped.
- Secrets by name only. Every merge, fix, task, split, and priority change is recorded with evidence on this issue; a change that cannot be verified by read-back did not happen.

items.body:
## Problem

`FileReadExecutor` enforces the selected-root boundary by canonicalizing a requested path and checking `starts_with(root)`, but then it checks metadata and opens the returned pathname in separate filesystem operations (`pkgs/id/crates/id-native-shell/src/providers.rs`, `resolve` and `execute`). If a writable directory entry is replaced with a symlink after `canonicalize()` returns but before `File::open()`, the later metadata/open follows the replacement outside the granted root. The read can therefore disclose bytes that the local user did not grant.

This is a race, not ordinary traversal: the requester needs the provider to be enabled and an attacker must be able to mutate a path component under the selected root concurrently. In that threat model, a remote world participant can supply the read request while the local filesystem writer races the operation. The existing symlink-escape test covers a stable symlink, not a replacement between check and use.

A temporary filesystem probe mirroring the current canonicalize → containment check → metadata → open sequence observed an outside-file read after successful in-root canonicalization while another thread swapped the requested entry between a regular file and an outside-pointing symlink. No repository code was changed.

## Required behavior

The file must be opened in a way that keeps resolution beneath the selected root through the actual open, and validation/read must use that same opened handle. Do not rely on canonicalize-then-open path checks for the security boundary.

## Acceptance criteria

- Add a deterministic regression test for a path/symlink replacement at the check/open boundary; the executor must never return outside-root bytes.
- Validate regular-file status and read bytes from the same opened file handle.
- Preserve reads of ordinary in-root files and the documented in-root symlink behavior; stable outside symlinks, traversal, and non-files remain refused.
- Use an OS-supported beneath-root open primitive or equivalent directory-handle traversal, with a documented safe fallback on supported platforms.

items.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#47 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #181

Backlog. Findings: `pkgs/mcpx/docs/opencode-plugin.md` §2 and §4.

**v1 plugins do not load in opencode v2** — no shim, no fallback (`packages/core/src/plugin/module.ts:60-73`). v2 needs a rewrite against `{id, setup}`, not a port.

What changes, each better than the v1 equivalent:

| v1 today | v2 |
| --- | --- |
| `shell.env` per command (carries sessionID) | `shell.create.before` has **no sessionID** → use `PUT /api/experimental/session/:id/environment` once per session |
| `experimental.chat.system.transform` | `session.hook("context")` → `event.system` (or a budgeted catalog in `event.tools`, diffed between turns) |
| `tool` map, un-namespaced | `tool.transform(e => e.add(...))` with a namespace |
| `tool.execute.after` sees success only | union on `status` — record failures too |
| state file for the remembered daemon | `ctx.storage` |
| no way to answer MCP sampling | `ctx.generate.text` — the plugin can answer mcpx's sampling questions |
| `$` for the CLI | gone — and nothing is lost: since #53 (closes #44) the plugin reaches the daemon over the unix socket and spawns `mcpx --json status` only as rung 4, the last fallback (`plugin/opencode/README.md:83-110`, `plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts`); `backend: v1` never spawns and `bin: ""` forbids it. In v2, drop rung 4 or keep it through `node:child_process`, which `daemon.ts` already imports |
| subdirectory to hide helpers from the loader | unnecessary; only `default` is read |

Also new in v2 and worth using: `mcp.transform` (register a *filtered* server set per session), `permission.hook("evaluate")` (real, unlike v1's dead `permission.ask`), promise-based TUI `select()` for the daemon picker.

**Also:** opencode v2's MCP client sends `_meta["ai.opencode/sessionID"]` on tool calls (`packages/core/src/mcp/client.ts:278`). When opencode v2 talks to mcpx as an MCP server, mcpx should read that for session attribution and leasing — no environment injection needed at all on that path.

Depends on: #44 (closed, fixed in #53 — the binary-free core exists).

Since this was filed (checked at 05c78b2):

- **#171's guard covers a v2 port automatically.** `TestThePluginReadsNoUndeclaredSetting`
  (`internal/settings/consumed_test.go:209-236`) scans every `plugin/**/*.ts(x)` except tests
  (`pluginSources`, `:288-320`), so a v2 plugin anywhere under `plugin/` must honour only variables declared in
  `pluginSettings()` (`internal/settings/plugin.go:18`). #171 also wired `plugin.discoveryRetry` and declared
  `plugin.remember`/`plugin.annotate`; the v2 port keeps all three.
- **The dead `permission.ask` hook** is recorded among the "declared but did nothing" incidents
  (`docs/declared-but-unread.md:8-12`, #75's PR body); nothing in the v1 plugin is built on it
  (`docs/plugin-discovery.md:144-145`). v2's `permission.hook("evaluate")` is the real one.
- The opencode-side line references above (`packages/core/src/plugin/module.ts:60-73`,
  `packages/core/src/mcp/client.ts:278`) are against opencode's `v2` branch and were not re-checked in this pass.

No real choice: v1 plugins do not load in v2, so the only question is when. The table above is the design.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** L (a rewrite against `{id, setup}`, not a port) · **Impact** med-high — nil while v1 is what runs,
total once v2 is (the v1 plugin does not load at all).

Related: #48 (the harness-free core this adapter sits on), #80 and #82 (the extension side; the same `/v1`
back-channel), #87 (`ctx.storage` replaces the remembered-daemon file; its lifetime follows #87's rule).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

items.body:
## Summary

Expand #2046 (serverless edition — `id` on Cloudflare Workers) with the storage decision it left open: what is the backing store for `id` when it runs on Workers, and can the answer be more than one store?

This is a design investigation, not an implementation ticket. Its deliverable is a decision-ready comparison of **Cloudflare D1 vs Turso (libSQL) vs offering both**, a recommendation with the conditions that would flip it, and follow-on design tickets (see Decomposition sketch) detailed enough to be broken into implementation work without re-litigating the choice.

Relates to: #2046 (serverless edition on Cloudflare Workers), #806 (F12.13 journal replication — read replicas over a signed stream).

## Why this matters

The serverless edition promises `id` with no server to run. That promise lives or dies on the store underneath it:

- Every `id` invariant — identity, capability grants, journal / event history, world state — has to survive on a store whose consistency, replication, and failure model were designed for edge web apps, not necessarily for a signed, replicated journal.
- Picking the wrong store does not just cost performance; it can silently weaken the journal's guarantees (ordering, durability, replay) or lock the serverless edition into a cost / limits shape that only appears at scale.
- Conversely, supporting two stores doubles the storage-abstraction surface forever. "Both" must be justified, bounded, and priced — not adopted as an avoidance of deciding.

## Options to compare

### A. D1 only

- Native to Cloudflare: Workers binding, no extra vendor, no extra credentials for the operator.
- SQLite semantics; single-primary with read replication where available. Evaluate consistency model in detail: write consistency, read-your-writes within a session, replica lag, and what happens across regions.
- Fit for the `id` journal (#806): can the signed journal be stored, ordered, and replicated with the guarantees #806 assumes? Where does D1 replication help, and where does the signed stream have to do its own work regardless?
- Limits: database size, row / query limits, Time Travel / point-in-time recovery, backup / export story for an operator who wants to leave Cloudflare.

### B. Turso (libSQL) only

- libSQL as a SQLite fork with replication as a first-class feature (embedded replicas, primary replication). Evaluate the same consistency questions as D1, plus embedded-replica sync latency and offline behaviour.
- Fit for #806: does libSQL replication compose with — or conflict with — replication over a signed stream? Two replication systems moving the same data is a hazard to name explicitly.
- Operational shape: an external dependency and account even in the "serverless" edition; self-hosted sqld as an escape hatch; what that does to the "just deploy to Workers" story.
- Cost and limits at hobby, small-community, and large-world scales.

### C. Both — per-world or per-deployment choice

- A storage-backend abstraction with D1 and Turso as interchangeable implementations, chosen per deployment, or finer: per world.
- Price the abstraction honestly: which `id` storage operations must be in the common subset, what backend-specific features are then forbidden, how migrations between backends work (export journal → replay into the other store?), and how tests / CI cover two backends without doubling flakiness.
- Per-world choice adds a routing / metadata question: where is the "which store holds this world" fact itself stored, and what happens when a world's store is unreachable?
- State the decision rule for when "both" is worth it (e.g. operator sovereignty, an existing Turso estate, D1 limits hit in practice) vs when it is speculative generality.

## Comparison axes (required in the deliverable)

For each option, address every axis — "unknown, needs spike" is an acceptable entry, an omitted axis is not:

1. **Consistency & ordering** — write consistency, cross-region behaviour, session guarantees, ordering available to the journal.
2. **Replication / journal fit (#806)** — how store replication interacts with signed-stream replication; single-writer assumptions; conflict and fork behaviour.
3. **Cost shape** — free / entry tier, per-read / per-write / per-row pricing, storage pricing, egress; modelled at three scales (single user, small community, large public world). Include the cost of the Workers tier needed in each case.
4. **Limits & ceilings** — DB size, request / query limits, connection model from Workers, cold-start and latency profile by region.
5. **Local-dev story** — local D1 (Wrangler / Miniflare) vs local libSQL / sqld; can a developer run the full serverless edition offline? Seed / fixture / reset ergonomics; parity between local and deployed behaviour and known divergences.
6. **Durability, backup & exit** — backup, point-in-time recovery, export in an open format, migration off the platform; data-loss windows.
7. **Security & tenancy** — credentials / bindings, per-world isolation, row-level isolation assumptions, encryption-at-rest story, what a compromised Worker can reach.
8. **Operational burden** — what the operator must provision, monitor, and pay for; failure modes visible to end users.

## Non-goals

- Implementing either backend (this issue decides and decomposes; implementation is follow-on work).
- Re-designing the journal itself (#806 owns the signed-stream design); this issue only evaluates store fit against it.
- Non-serverless storage (self-hosted edition storage is out of scope except where the abstraction in option C would leak into it — flag any such leak explicitly).
- Choosing other serverless platforms (Workers is the #2046 premise).

## Acceptance criteria for the design deliverable

- [ ] A comparison document covering options A / B / C across all eight axes above, linked from this issue.
- [ ] A stated recommendation, the evidence behind it, and the conditions that would reverse it.
- [ ] An explicit statement of which journal guarantees (#806) each store preserves, weakens, or requires compensating design for.
- [ ] If "both" is recommended: the common storage contract, the choice granularity (per-deployment vs per-world), and the migration path between backends.
- [ ] Cost model at the three named scales, with assumptions listed.
- [ ] Follow-on design tickets filed from the Decomposition sketch (or the sketch revised with reasons).

## Decomposition sketch

Follow-on design tickets to be filed from this issue (indicative; revise during the work):

1. Design: storage contract for the serverless edition — the minimal `id` storage interface both backends must satisfy (journal append/read, world state, indexes).
2. Design / spike: D1 journal fit — ordering, sessions, and replication behaviour against the #806 signed-stream requirements, with a small proof of concept.
3. Design / spike: Turso / libSQL journal fit — embedded replicas and primary replication composed with #806, with a small proof of concept.
4. Design: local-dev parity for the serverless edition — Wrangler/Miniflare vs local sqld, fixtures, and the offline developer workflow.
5. Design: backend choice & migration — per-deployment vs per-world selection, where the routing fact lives, and export/replay migration between D1 and Turso.
6. Design: cost & limits guardrails — quotas, backpressure, and operator-visible warnings when a world approaches D1 / Turso ceilings.
7. Design: backup, recovery & exit for serverless storage — point-in-time recovery, open-format export, and leaving Cloudflare / Turso.

## Open questions

- Does #806's signed stream actually need store-level replication at all, or is store replication redundant (or actively harmful) once the journal replicates itself?
- Is per-world backend choice a real operator need, or is per-deployment enough? What evidence would distinguish the two?
- What is the largest world (events, state size, write rate) the serverless edition intends to support — and does either store's ceiling rule it out before cost does?
- How much D1 / Turso behaviour can only be learned from a running spike vs vendor documentation, and which claims in the comparison are documentation-only?
- If both are supported, who owns keeping the second backend honest — CI matrix, contract tests, or manual verification per release?
- Does Turso's self-hosted sqld option blur the line between the serverless and self-hosted editions in a useful way, or create a third, accidental edition?

items.body:
Follow-up from the design note in [#4962](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4962) (`doc/2026-11-03T14-55-00Z_design_id4630_oversized_replication_entries.md`), which chose **bounded checkpoint at write time** for [#4630](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/4630). Implementation issue — the fix for #4630 itself; #4630 closes when this merges.

## Problem

`WorldCore::checkpoint_entries` (`pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:1063-1200`) emits the whole compacted world as **one** `JournalEntry::Checkpoint`. Nothing bounds its size:

- the program snapshot `String` (passed in from `world/actor.rs:275`) has no `WorldLimits` bound (`snapshot_bytes` bounds only the client-facing snapshot's event selection, `core.rs:2063`);
- retained `events` (≤ `retained_events`, default 1024, each ≤ `input_bytes` 16 KiB, hex-encoded entity inputs double that);
- `admin_history` (≤ min(`retained_events`, 4096)).

One such entry over `MAX_REPLICATION_PAYLOAD_BYTES` (256 KiB, `pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs:79`) makes `split_entry_payload` return `PayloadTooLarge` and `send_snapshot` (`world_replication_net.rs:206-243`) fail before the first frame. No other entry kind can grow unboundedly (chat ≤ 2 KiB, input ≤ 16 KiB, participant/ceiling/schedule entries small, `open_presence` capped at 4096 IDs), so bounding the checkpoint bounds every entry.

## Required change

Split the checkpoint into bounded part entries at compaction time, mirroring the existing pre-`Checkpoint` entry pattern (`CapsCeiling`, `ScheduleSet`, `Isolation`, `ExecutionProfile`, transfer entries):

- new part entry kinds for the program snapshot, retained events, and admin history, each `{ sequence, part_index, part_count, ... }`, split by **encoded** size (`serde_json::to_vec` of the assembled part) at UTF-8 boundaries for the string;
- `MAX_CHECKPOINT_PART_BYTES = 192 * 1024` — deliberately below the 256 KiB payload bound, leaving headroom for the part's scalar fields and JSON framing;
- `Checkpoint` keeps scalars plus `open_presence` (≈86 KiB worst case at the 4096-ID cap, under the part bound);
- restore assembles parts for the same `sequence`, refusing missing / duplicate / out-of-order / mismatched `part_count` parts, and applies exactly today's state;
- bump `JOURNAL_VERSION` to 6 and map the new kinds in `journal_version_required_by`, per the existing header-bump contract (`world/mod.rs:980-1060`);
- keep `MAX_REPLICATION_PAYLOAD_BYTES` and the envelope at v1 — **no wire change, no envelope bump, no `ReplicationTracker::accept` change**.

Constraint: a checkpoint that would exceed the part bound must be split, never skipped or truncated — compaction may not silently keep the untrimmed journal for size reasons, except for the already-documented open-presence limit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A compacted journal from a world whose program snapshot is > 256 KiB contains no entry over `MAX_CHECKPOINT_PART_BYTES`, and `restore` reconstructs the identical `WorldCore` state (snapshot bytes, retained events, admin history, presence, transfers, schedules, profile).
- [ ] **#4630 regression test:** the same oversized-Checkpoint journal image round-trips the feed path — `journal_entry_line` per entry → `split_entry_payload` (no `PayloadTooLarge`) → `ReplicationEnvelope::snapshot`/`tail` + `send_snapshot` framing → `ReplicationTracker::accept` — and the accepted cursor equals the sender's final cursor; the received journal `restore`s to the same state.
- [ ] Boundary tests: a part of exactly `MAX_CHECKPOINT_PART_BYTES` passes; one byte over is split, not errored; a multi-byte UTF-8 character is never cut mid-character.
- [ ] Journal-version tests: a v6 journal is refused by a version-5 reader at the header check; a journal needing only v1-v5 keeps its existing version.
- [ ] `cargo test -p id --lib world::replication` passes.
- [ ] The `world_store` replication feed tests pass (they build snapshot bytes through the same path).
- [ ] The existing journal-version / restore / compaction suites pass (`cargo test -p id --lib world`).
- [ ] The module doc of `pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs` states the resulting per-entry guarantee from the design note (every writer-emitted entry ≤ 192 KiB, hence ≤ one v1 payload frame), replacing "such an entry can never be replicated in v1".

## Out of scope

- Sub-entry fragmentation / continuation frames (rejected in the note: v1→v2 wire bump plus permanent receiver buffering for a writer-controlled entry kind).
- Raising `MAX_REPLICATION_PAYLOAD_BYTES` (deferred; it changes a receiver-side constant, so it is a compatibility decision).
- Legacy journals already holding an oversized `Checkpoint` — handled by the companion residual issue.

items.body:
## Problem

In the `id` web editor, the image node's `parseDOM` converts the `width`/`height` attributes with a bare `Number()` and the attrs declare no validation, so non-integer dimensions are stored verbatim and then silently dropped (or reinterpreted) downstream:

- `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:145-146` — `width: el.getAttribute("width") ? Number(el.getAttribute("width")) : null` (same for `height`). The image attrs at `editor.ts:125-126` are `{ default: null }` with no `validate`, unlike `ordered_list`'s `order` which at least declares `validate: "number"` (and still lets NaN through — #2005).
- `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:157-158` — `toDOM` emits the attr only `if (node.attrs.width)`: `NaN` and `0` are falsy, so they vanish; a fraction (`2.5`) or negative (`-5`) is emitted as the invalid attribute `width="2.5"` / `width="-5"`.
- `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:1953-1954` — on save, `json["attrs"]["width"].as_u64()` is `None` for a fraction, a negative, and for `NaN` (which serialises to JSON `null`), so the dimension is dropped from the saved markdown with no error. The Rust-side HTML parse (`markdown.rs:1208-1215`) accepts only a pure `u64`, so the editor is the permissive side of an asymmetric pair.
- `pkgs/id/web/src/image-node-view.ts:58-62` — the node view sets `img.style.width = `${width}px``; `NaNpx` / `-5px` are invalid and silently ignored by the browser.

## Verified this run (2026-10-28, main `38f1f00f`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-imgdim/`, the shipped `getAttrs` conversion copied verbatim; `editor.ts` sha256 `4340aef4…` identical on laptop and sandbox main), with the `toDOM` truthiness check and the save-side `as_u64()` semantics modelled from the shipped code:

- Control `width="200"` → parseDOM `200`, toDOM `"200"`, saved `200` ✓
- `width="200px"` → `NaN` → toDOM omits the attribute, saved `null` — dimension silently lost
- `width="50%"` → `NaN` → same silent loss
- `width="2.5"` → `2.5` → toDOM emits `width="2.5"`, saved `null` — lost on save
- `width="-5"` → `-5` → toDOM emits `width="-5"`, saved `null` — lost on save
- `width="abc"` → `NaN` → silently lost
- `width="0x10"` → `16` and `width="1e3"` → `1000` — silently *reinterpreted* as values the author never wrote (an HTML dimension attribute is a leading-digits value, not a JS numeric literal)

Pasted web content is the realistic source: images in copied HTML routinely carry `width="200px"`, percentage widths, or fractional/negative junk from CMS markup, and every one of those pastes loses its sizing on the next save without any signal.

## Why it matters

This is the same silent-coercion class as #2005 (ordered-list `start`) in the adjacent node of the same file, but with a different failure shape: the list renumbers, the image *loses its dimensions* (or gains ones nobody typed, `0x10` → 16). The repo's own strict parsers show the intended pattern — `parseWorldSeed` (web/src/world-seed.ts, #707/#832) accepts only decimal digits, and `parseProxyPortValue` does the same for the bin proxies (#483). The image attrs are an unhardened spot the earlier passes missed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Image `width`/`height` from `parseDOM` are either a non-negative integer or `null`: a value that is not a plain run of decimal digits (e.g. `200px`, `50%`, `2.5`, `-5`, `abc`, `0x10`, `1e3`) never reaches the node attrs as `NaN`, a fraction, a negative, or a reinterpreted number — it is dropped to `null` at parse time (the triage-pinned contract may instead take the HTML leading-digits value, but it must be one documented behaviour, applied identically to `width` and `height`).
- [ ] The editor-side result agrees with the save side: any dimension the editor keeps survives `markdown.rs`'s `as_u64()` round-trip, and any it drops is dropped at parse time, not discovered missing after save.
- [ ] Regression tests (web/src/editor.test.ts or a sibling) cover at least: `"200"` (kept), `"200px"`, `"50%"`, `"2.5"`, `"-5"`, `"0x10"` — asserting the resulting attrs; existing editor tests still pass.
- [ ] The fix is scoped to the image node (the ordered-list site is #2005's, already filed).

items.body:
Drew's ruling (2026-11-04): consolidate the fleet's tools into ONE multicall binary, `fleet`, as the single distribution unit — including the proxy (serve and connect) as domains of the binary itself — with compile-time capability-selected build variants.

## Why
Tonight's costs were distribution, not functionality: the repo-queue binary migration burned hours on PATH placement across 45 cron bodies, four worker instruction files, hooks, and two hosts; Atlas separately solved packaging, state-dir provisioning, and service wiring; every tool re-pays secret resolution and the sandbox↔laptop proxy transport. One artifact pays these once.

## Shape
- One Cargo workspace; each domain a crate (the atlas-search workspace — core/embed/proto/bin — and pkgs/id are the existence proofs). Domains at filing time: `search` (atlas), `queue` (repo-queue), `dispatch`, `proxy` (serve + connect), `broker` roles as designed.
- Multicall via argv0 (busybox-style): a `repo-queue` symlink to `fleet` behaves as repo-queue. Every existing call site keeps working untouched; `fleet <domain>` is the unified surface for humans and agents.
- Proxy integrated, used everywhere: `fleet proxy serve` is the broker (today's sandbox session broker + laptop listeners become one program in two roles); `fleet proxy connect` is the client half every location uses. `fleet init` autostarts the proxy, no-op if already running (Drew's standing directive).
- Capability-selected builds (Cargo features, compile-time): the flake publishes several attrs from the same source — e.g. full `fleet`, a serve-side build, and a TINY connect-only build carrying just the proxy client (unselected domains are absent from the artifact, not disabled — capability limits as a build property, mechanically enforced). Feature-gated CLI surface: each variant's --help shows only what it can do. The proxy wire protocol is the stable contract (versioned handshake + capability negotiation, atlas-proto discipline).
- Graceful stubs for missing capabilities: every variant compiles in the full domain registry (names + one-line descriptions — strings only), independent of feature selection. Dispatch: (a) a compiled-in domain runs; (b) a KNOWN but not-compiled domain produces a deliberate stub, not a parser error — message naming the missing capability and listing the capabilities this build DOES have (e.g. "this build does not include ‘queue’. Enabled capabilities: proxy-connect."), on stderr, with a distinct documented exit code (design note pins the code; distinct from generic errors so agents can branch on it). Applies equally to argv0 multicall invocation (a `repo-queue` symlink pointing at a connect-only bin gets the same stub naming ‘queue’). `--help` on any variant shows the full fleet surface with unavailable domains marked as not included in this build.
- Heavy domains stay lazy: no domain with large native deps (atlas/ONNX) may tax another domain's startup; dynamic loading at first use, as atlas-embed already does.
- Domains independently killable: config-level domain disable; during migration each domain crate stays buildable as a standalone binary (additive-first) so a bad domain can be pinned back without rolling back the world.

## Sequencing (constraints)
- Step 0 is a DESIGN NOTE (doc/ pattern from the atlas epic) — variant matrix, proxy protocol versioning, broker lifecycle, argv0 map, migration order — with a go/no-go gate before implementation steps are filed.
- Pilot domain: repo-queue (freshest binary, widest distribution pain, small surface). Proxy integration early (it is the distribution mechanism). Atlas joins LAST, at a natural seam after epic #5350 step 6 cutover — this epic must not destabilize the in-flight Atlas cutover or the fleet switch.
- Testing rule: every SHIPPED variant gets its own smoke test; the feature power set is not tested, the shipped matrix is.

## Open questions for the design
- Variant matrix: which builds ship (full / serve / connect-only / others?) and their exact feature sets.
- Proxy protocol: framing, versioning, capability negotiation, and how proxied PATH exposure works on connect (the repo-queue-on-PATH expectation).
- Broker state: what the serve side persists (warm tunnels, routing table) and its failure/restart semantics.
- Release mechanics: one version for all variants from one source tree; how a domain-scoped rollback works in practice.

## Acceptance criteria
- the fleet multicall binary ships with search, queue, dispatch, and proxy domains under capability-selected builds; child steps #5429-#5433 are all closed with evidence.
- No regression: existing tests/checks for the touched area remain green, and the change lands via PR referencing this issue.
- Evidence (PR link, test/CI output, or verification note) is posted on this issue before it is closed.

items.body:
## Summary

`get_serve_info()` decides whether the serve lock (`.iroh-serve.lock`) is stale by checking only that the recorded pid **exists** — `is_process_alive(pid)` is `kill(pid, 0) == 0` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:200-210`). It never checks that the process holding that pid is the serve that wrote the lock. When a serve dies without removing its lock (crash, `kill -9`, power loss) and the OS later hands that pid to an unrelated long-lived process, the lock passes the staleness check forever: `get_serve_info` returns the dead serve's `ServeInfo` (serve.rs:171-185), and every command that consults the lock first — `get` (commands/get.rs:101), `list` (commands/list.rs:72), `put`, `peers`, the REPL, the meta client (meta_client.rs:103) — tries to connect to the recorded addresses of a serve that no longer exists instead of falling back to opening the local store directly. The failure presents as a connection error against a phantom endpoint; nothing points at the lock file.

This is the reuse sibling of #2142, which covers sentinel pids read from disk (`0`, `u32::MAX`) answering "alive" for no process at all. #2142's fix (refuse non-positive / out-of-range pids) does nothing here: a reused pid is an ordinary in-range pid held by a real process — just the wrong one.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `a9df3018`)

The gate in `get_serve_info` is straight-line: read the lock JSON → parse `ServeInfo` (serve.rs:130-141) → `is_process_alive(info.pid)` → `Some(info)`, else delete the lock and return `None`. The only staleness test is pid existence.

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-pidreuse/`; `is_process_alive` copied verbatim from serve.rs:200-210 with `libc::kill` spelled as the FFI call it wraps; serve.rs md5 `9a3eba3e2c09114e28d6932f8a102fea` identical in the sandbox and laptop clones):

```text
pid 2086858: comm=sleep state=S
gate accepts lock while pid is held by sleep: true
gate accepts same lock after sleep exits:    false
RESULT: the lock staleness check tests pid existence, not serve identity
```

The probe spawns an unrelated `sleep 120` (verified live and running via `/proc/<pid>/comm` = `sleep`, state `S` — not a zombie, not an `id serve`), writes a lock naming that pid with a dead endpoint's addresses, and the gate accepts it; the moment the sleeper exits, the same lock is refused. So the check cannot distinguish "serve alive" from "any process alive with that pid".

## Why it matters

Serve discovery is the front door for most CLI commands in a served directory. A crashed serve plus ordinary pid reuse (routine on long-uptime machines and in containers with small pid namespaces, where wraparound is fast) turns a recoverable state into persistent, misleading connection failures in that directory until a human deletes `.iroh-serve.lock` by hand — the same wedge class as #2142, reached by a mundane path rather than a corrupt file.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The staleness check verifies the pid holder is the serve that wrote the lock (e.g. the lock records the serve's start time / exe identity and `get_serve_info` compares it, or an equivalent identity check), so a lock whose pid was reused by an unrelated process is treated as stale: removed, and `None` returned.
- [ ] A lock written by a live serve behaves exactly as before (discovery still succeeds against the running serve).
- [ ] A lock with an ordinary dead pid behaves exactly as before (removed, `None`).
- [ ] Regression tests cover: live serve pid accepted; dead pid refused; live **unrelated** pid refused.
- [ ] The fix states how it behaves on non-Unix platforms, where `is_process_alive` currently always answers `true`.

Dedup: #2142 (open) covers sentinel pids `0`/`u32::MAX` only; its acceptance criteria do not include pid-reuse identity. Searches for `serve lock pid reuse`, `is_process_alive`, and `stale lock` returned no other covering issue.

Follow-up to #2229 (method 2 of 3). Method 3 — the opencode-route provider front — shipped as the priority build (PR #2250, live-proven). This method was descoped by Drew on 2026-10-29 to a follow-up: **sometime soon / when an OpenClaw-origin workload needs to spawn subagents from headless/CLI sessions.**

## What it adds

`sessions_spawn` exposed to headless/CLI OpenClaw sessions, so a CLI-driven agent turn can spawn subagents — including ACP-runtime targets such as the `opencode-acp` entry (the method-1 follow-up), whose live proof depends on this surface.

## Determination (already made, 2026-10-29 — this is a packaging patch, not config)

- In the pinned OpenClaw 2026.10.7 dist, `createSessionsSpawnTool` is gated by `!embedded || options?.allowGatewaySubagentBinding === true` (chunk `openclaw-tools-QaFYBVQi.mjs`). `isEmbeddedMode()` is a process-local flag set only by `EmbeddedTuiBackend.start()`, and `openclaw agent` CLI turns run through that embedded backend even when gateway-attached. `allowGatewaySubagentBinding: true` is passed only by gateway/channel-side runners. **No config key or tool profile feeds either flag** — the tool sits in the "sessions" group with profiles `["coding","messaging"]`; profile is not the blocker.
- Empirically absent on every surface tried: CLI via the live gateway, CLI `--local`, and a server-side `chat.send` turn (the agent reported sessions_spawn is not in its loadable tool set; the deferred-tool layer answers `select:sessions_spawn` with "No deferred tool matched").
- Route: nix-openclaw's instance options expose `gatewayPath` + `gatewayPnpmDepsHash`; when `gatewayPath` is set, the module builds the gateway from that source. So: commit a `.patch` against the pinned upstream source flipping the gate condition, wire `gatewayPath` to a patched-source derivation in the fleet config, and document plainly that it is a source patch carried by the packaging, not an upstream config option.

## Proof when built

Patch a copied dist tree first for a fast mechanism proof (spawn with `agentId="opencode"` and `agentId="opencode-acp"` → check `acp_sessions` in the OpenClaw state plus a new row in OpenCode `session_v2`), then land the durable source patch.
